title: Numbers in letters
hook: each letter has a number value; chai is eighteen

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sh-M: shem, a name, and Shemot, the book of names. Your line was names matter. Did you ask someone how to say theirs? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-three.

Three hundred and eighteen. That's the number Genesis gives when Abram hears his nephew Lot has been carried off by raiding kings: "he armed his trained servants, born in his own house, three hundred and eighteen," and went after them. An oddly exact number for a rescue party. A reader could pass right over it. One rabbi in the Talmud didn't. He looked at three hundred and eighteen and saw a person. To see what he saw, you need one fact about the Hebrew alphabet: its letters can also be read as numbers. Today's word is what happens when you add them up.
screen: `ABRAM'S RESCUE PARTY.` → `THREE HUNDRED AND EIGHTEEN.` → `ONE RABBI SAW A PERSON.`

segments.voice: Gematria. In Hebrew, each letter carries a number. Alef is one, bet is two, and so on up to yod, which is ten; then the tens, then the hundreds. So any word has a sum. Turn it four ways. First, one you may have seen on a necklace. Chai, alive, is spelled with two letters: chet, eight, and yod, ten. Together, eighteen. That is why eighteen carries a quiet meaning in Jewish life. Some families give gifts in multiples of eighteen, a way of wishing someone life along with the money. Second, back to Abram. The Talmud records a teacher who said those three hundred and eighteen men were really one man: Eliezer, Abram's servant. Add the letters of the name Eliezer, and they come to three hundred and eighteen. Read that way, Abram went to the rescue with one faithful helper, and the number was a name in disguise. Third, a sense of proportion. Pirkei Avot sets gematria in its place. Rabbi Eliezer ben Chisma calls certain detailed laws the essentials, and calls gematria, along with the study of the heavens, the after-courses of wisdom. The side dishes. Delicious, worth having, but not the meal. Even inside the tradition, the game is given its place at the table. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary day. Gematria trains a reader to notice. A number that looks like filler might be worth a second look. A word might hold more than its first meaning. The letters are not only sounds; they count, and they can be counted. Letters count.
screen: `EVERY LETTER IS A NUMBER.` · `CHAI: EIGHT AND TEN.` · `318: ONE MAN NAMED ELIEZER?` · `THE AFTER-COURSES OF WISDOM.` · then, large: `LETTERS COUNT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: add up your name. If you know how your name, or a Hebrew name you love, is written in Hebrew letters, find each letter's value and add them, slowly, one by one. If you don't, start with chai: chet is eight, yod is ten. Say the sum to yourself. Then let the arithmetic go and sit with the word itself. What does it hold for you? A person, a memory, a hope? The point isn't the total. It's the slow attention, letter by letter, that the game asks of a reader. If you pray, you can give thanks for the life the word chai names. The bell holds the time.
screen: `YOUR NAME, LETTER BY LETTER.` · `OR CHAI: EIGHT AND TEN.` · `LET THE SUM GO. KEEP THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Gematria. Reading Hebrew letters as numbers, and finding meaning in the sums. Chai is eighteen; Abram's three hundred and eighteen, one reading says, is Eliezer. Today's word.
Your line: letters count. Today, when a number turns up, on a receipt, a clock, a page, give it a second look before you move on. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-three.

original.note: Hebrew: reading letters as numbers; chai, חי, adds up to eighteen.

trapdoor: what you thought: numbers and letters are separate things.
what it means: in Hebrew every letter is also a number, so every word has a sum, like chai, eighteen.
what a scholar hears: the Talmud reads Abram's 318 as Eliezer, and Pirkei Avot files gematria among the after-courses of wisdom.

notes: Letter values (alef 1, bet 2 … yod 10, then tens, then hundreds) and chai = chet 8 + yod 10 = 18 are standard; the index states chai is eighteen. Confirm.

Nedarim 32a: Rami bar Abba (some versions attribute differently) says Eliezer alone went, since Eliezer equals 318 (alef 1, lamed 30, yod 10, ayin 70, zayin 7, resh 200). Also Bereshit Rabbah 43:2. Confirm attribution; the script says 'a teacher'.

Pirkei Avot 3:18 (3:23 in some numberings): Rabbi Eliezer ben Chisma: kinnim and the laws of niddah are the essentials (gufei) of halakhah; astronomy (tekufot) and gematriaot are the after-courses (parpera'ot) of wisdom. Paraphrased. Confirm.
The custom of giving gifts in multiples of eighteen is described as something 'some families' do. Confirm.
Original: unpointed spelling גימטריה given; stress shown in common English pronunciation (modern Israeli stress may fall differently). Confirm.
Editor pass: cut an unsourced generalization about what the rabbis enjoyed and knew about gematria; the line now only restates what Pirkei Avot 3:18 says.
